extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, and scholars of anthropology and humor studies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and conceptual criteria for conducting a cross-cultural, anthropological analysis of humor and laughter, focusing on stimuli, cognitive appraisal, and social/cultural responses. Emphasizes formulating theory through comparative evidence and making cultural codes explicit for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three elements of humor (sources, cognition, behavioral responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: It appears that three elements need to be considered: 1) sources that act as potential stimuli; 2) the cognitive and intellectual activity responsible for the perception and evaluation of these sources leading to humor experience; and 3) behavioral responses that are expressed as smiling or laughter or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These attributes generally occur sequentially; the framework identifies stimulus → mental activity → observable response as the core dimensions to address when analyzing humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential process model (stimulus → appraisal → response)
rubrics_metrics.description: These attributes of the conceptualization of humor generally occur sequentially as I have ordered them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying or describing humor, map events onto this sequence and consider how each stage transforms or mediates the next; use the sequence to trace causes and consequences of humor episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of cognitive appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: However, it is the second phase, the mental activity experienced by an individual, that is most crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give special analytic weight to perception and evaluation processes (cognitive/intellectual activity) when explaining whether and how stimuli become humorous; methodological emphasis should be on understanding mental operations, not only stimuli or responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor is culture-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Two axioms underlie my discussion, namely, that humor is by and large culture based...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses must situate humor within cultural knowledge and codes — what is humorous in one culture may not be in another; treat cultural context as constitutive, not merely background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as conceptual and methodological tool
rubrics_metrics.description: ...and that humor can be a major conceptual and methodological tool for gaining insights into cultural systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor data to reveal values, norms, and implicit cultural patterns; treat jokes, laughter, and comic practices as evidence-bearing phenomena for cultural analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cultural comparative objective
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall pursue two broad objectives: 1) the exploration by cross-cultural comparison of the interdependence of humor and socio-cultural factors in societies around the world, and the formulation of generalizations based on such an investigation;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies that compare multiple societies to identify interdependencies and to support generalizations; avoid single-culture-only claims when the aim is comparative understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory-building objective (formulate theoretical propositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: 2) the setting forth of theoretical propositions regarding the similar and different ways in which humor is linked to socio-cultural factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond description, explicitly derive propositions and hypotheses from comparative data; use empirical patterns to construct mid-level theories about humor's cultural roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key research questions for anthropological humor studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions asked: Are there cross-culturally shared ways in which humor stimuli are generated and humor appreciated? Are there categories and types of humor that occur in many societies? Does humor serve similar purposes in many societies? Do similar behaviors, objects, institutions, and so forth across cultures serve as stimuli of humor? Do cultures share similar attitudes toward the need, desirability, occurrence, and use of humor in certain social events?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these specific questions to frame empirical inquiry and data collection; they function as evaluative criteria for whether a study addresses the comparative and functional dimensions of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on external stimuli and cultural niche
rubrics_metrics.description: My discussion principally focuses on the external stimuli of humor and responses to it. Even if humor is a cognitive experience for an individual, it must have a cultural niche; it cannot occur in a vacuum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize analysis of externally observable stimuli and their culturally-specific meanings; document the cultural contexts that make stimuli intelligible as humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine sequential events and consequences at individual and societal levels
rubrics_metrics.description: I also explore the nature of sequential events of humor and its consequences at both the individual and societal level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both micro-level (individual experience, laughter, social interaction) and macro-level (social functions, institutions, norms) consequences; trace how humor episodes scale from personal to societal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-theoretical and prospective approach: critique and propose theories
rubrics_metrics.description: I pursue both meta-theoretical and prospective approaches, critically examining the theories of other scholars regarding the causes, facets, and effects of humor phenomena. In addition I formulate new theories and explanations by way of propositions and hypotheses after analyzing the interconnections between humor and other socio-cultural dimensions to determine how they influence the nature and function of humor at the culture-specific and general levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine critical review of existing literature with forward-looking hypothesis generation; use empirical interconnections to both test other theories and to build alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make implicit cultural codes explicit for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Answers to such questions should make explicit the implicit patterned aspects of a cultural code so that they can be subjected to verification and confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting humor data, articulate the underlying cultural norms and categories that render stimuli humorous; explicitly state cultural standards used in interpretation to allow verification by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural membership requirement for humor perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals are not conscious of this requirement, because they already possess the cultural knowledge to which they compare the humor-generating stimuli. An individual who is not a member of a specific culture and therefore has not internalized its behavioral patterns and value system may not experience humor, lacking the necessary standard for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider researchers' and audiences' cultural backgrounds when interpreting data; acknowledge limits of outsider comprehension and account for potential non-recognition of humor by those outside the culture studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for selecting humor-related ethnographic data (mentioned)
rubrics_metrics.description: This introductory chapter ... describing criteria for selecting humor-related ethnographic data and the limitations of such a study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states that criteria for selecting ethnographic data exist but does not enumerate them in this excerpt; any empirical study should include explicit sampling/selection criteria for humor data and discuss limitations.
